introduction.title: What the Barbell Row Builds
paragraphs: The barbell row has you hinge forward with a flat back and pull the bar from arm's length to your lower chest or upper stomach. It builds the lats, upper back and rear shoulders, and it strengthens the same back position you hold in every deadlift.
A strong row balances the pressing in a typical program. It supports healthy shoulders, gives your bench press a stable base to push from, and helps you keep the bar close on heavy pulls.
Hold your torso angle steady and let your arms and back do the work.

faqItems.question: What is the difference between a barbell row and a Pendlay row?
faqItems.answer: A Pendlay row returns the bar to the floor every rep with the torso close to parallel, so each rep starts from a dead stop. A standard barbell row keeps the bar hanging between reps, usually with the torso a little more upright.

faqItems.question: Should I use an overhand or underhand grip for barbell rows?
faqItems.answer: Both work. An overhand grip emphasises the upper back, while an underhand grip brings in more biceps and usually lets you lift a little more. Choose one as your main row and log it consistently so your progress is easy to compare.

faqItems.question: Where should the bar touch when I row?
faqItems.answer: Aim for your lower chest or upper stomach, depending on your arm length and torso angle. The bar should travel in a fairly straight line up from the middle of your foot.

faqItems.question: How do I keep my lower back strong while rowing?
faqItems.answer: Brace before the first rep, keep your back flat, and hold the same torso angle through the set. If your hips start swinging to move the weight, take a little off and keep the reps controlled.

faqItems.question: How often should I train barbell rows?
faqItems.answer: Once or twice a week works well for most lifters, often on the same days as bench press or overhead pressing.
